subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 7 of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is all about the machines that computers control — and the most exciting of these is the robot. The big idea to hold onto the whole way through is simple: a computer or a robot only ever does what its instructions tell it to do. It does not think for itself. If we give it clear, correct steps in the right order, it does the job well. If our steps are wrong, it does the wrong thing — and it will not notice or fix it for us.

First, you learn that computers save our work as files, and that there are different types of file — text, audio (sound), image (picture), video, and games. Second, you learn that computers can control machines: a computer-controlled device takes an input and makes an output that tells the machine what to do. Third, you meet the Internet of Things — everyday objects like fridges and lightbulbs joined to the internet, called smart devices. Fourth, you learn what robots do, especially in factories: they move materials, build things, and check that work is good. The big skill on top is to give a robot a clear sequence of commands to guide it to a goal — and to spot and fix a command that is wrong.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 3 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Name the main types of file on a computer (text, audio, image, video, game) and give an example of each.
Explain that a computer-controlled device takes an input and makes an output that tells a machine what to do.
Name some common Internet of Things (smart) devices and say that they connect to the internet.
Explain that a robot is a computer-controlled device that follows a program, and name what robots do when making things (handle materials, build, inspect).
Give a robot a clear sequence of commands (Forward, Turn Left, Turn Right) to guide it to a goal.
Find and fix a command that is wrong, and understand that a robot cannot think for itself.
In Scratch, join blocks in the right order to move a robot sprite to a goal.

concepts.title: Files on a computer
concepts.explanation:
Computers save our work as files. There are different types of file — text, audio (sound), image (picture), video (moving pictures), and games. Every file has a name so we can find it again, and files are kept in folders, just like papers at home.

At home we keep important papers in folders so we can find them. A computer does the same. Everything we make on a computer is saved as a file, and each file has its own name.
concepts.example: Find one real example of files on a computer around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tell the difference between an image (a still picture) and a video (moving pictures)? Can you name the file type for a photo, a song and a typed letter?

concepts.title: Computers control machines
concepts.explanation:
Computers do more than save files — they can control machines. A computer-controlled device takes an input (something that goes in) and makes an output (something that comes out) which tells the machine what to do. The same machine can be made to do different jobs by changing its program.

When a car drives up, someone presses a button. That is the input. A little computer then lifts the barrier. That is the output.
concepts.example: The computer told the machine what to do. Use the car-park gate.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you point to a computer-controlled device in real life, such as a microwave or a washing machine? Can you give an input and say the output it causes?

concepts.title: The Internet of Things
concepts.explanation:
The internet joins lots of computers together. The Internet of Things means joining lots of everyday objects to the internet too. These objects are called smart devices. Because they are on the internet, they can send and receive information, and we can control them from a phone.

Compare an ordinary fridge with a smart one. A normal fridge just keeps food cold.
concepts.example: A smart fridge is joined to the internet — it can notice the milk is finished and order more all by itself. Things joined to the internet like this are smart devices.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you see that a plain object like a wooden chair or a paper book cannot join the internet? Can you name a smart device and say that it connects to the internet?

concepts.title: Robots follow commands (the Robot Game)
concepts.explanation:
A robot is a computer-controlled device. It is given a program — a set of instructions — and it does exactly what the program says. In factories, robots have three main jobs: they handle materials (move boxes from place to place), you build things (join parts together), and they inspect (check that the work is good and safe). The most important idea of the whole unit lives here: a robot cannot think for itself. It only does what we tell it.
 — play the Robot Game. Mark a start spot on the floor and place a goal a few steps away (a book for the library, or a cup for the well).
concepts.example: One child is the robot. The robot-child does exactly one command at a time — no more, no less.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that a wrong command gives a wrong result — and that it is our job, not the robot's, to make the commands right? Does you give one clear command at a time, in order?

concepts.title: Give the robot a sequence on screen (Scratch)
concepts.explanation:
We can give a robot a sequence of commands on the computer too. In Scratch we join blocks in the right order to move a robot to a goal. Just like the robot game, the order of the blocks matters.

Open Scratch at scratch.mit.edu and click Create on the projector. Click the little trash can on the cat to delete it, then click the Add Sprite button and choose the Robot sprite (any sprite is fine if you cannot find the robot).
concepts.example: Explain that the middle of the stage is where the well is, and we will write a sequence of blocks to walk the robot there. Use the same kind of movement block you met with the balloon in Unit 1: change x by ( ) slides the sprite to the right, and change y by ( ) slides it up.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you join the blocks in order and run the program with the green flag?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Any one of: move (handle) materials; build (join) things; inspect (check) the work.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in robots follow commands (the robot game), and give one example of your own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A robot is a computer-controlled device. It is given a program — a set of instructions — and it does exactly what the program says. In factories, robots have three main jobs: they handle materials (move boxes from place to place), you build things (join parts together), and they inspect (check that the work is good and safe). The most important idea of the whole unit lives here: a robot cannot think for itself. It only does what we tell it.
 — play the Robot Game. Mark a start spot on the floor and place a goal a few steps away (a book for the library, or a cup for the well).

project.title: Unit 7 Project: Computers and Robots
project.brief: Bring together everything from Computers and Robots into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your computers and robots project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I wrote clear commands to guide the robot through the maze to the well.
My robot never landed on a wall.
I found the square where Maya's robot bumped, and I fixed her commands.
In Scratch, my robot moved to the well.
I can explain that a robot only does what its commands say.

selfAssessment: I can name the main types of file on a computer (text, audio, image, video, game) and give an example of each.
I can explain that a computer-controlled device takes an input and makes an output that tells a machine what to do.
I can name some common Internet of Things (smart) devices and say that they connect to the internet.
I can explain that a robot is a computer-controlled device that follows a program, and name what robots do when making things (handle materials, build, inspect).
I can give a robot a clear sequence of commands (Forward, Turn Left, Turn Right) to guide it to a goal.
I can find and fix a command that is wrong, and understand that a robot cannot think for itself.
I can in Scratch, join blocks in the right order to move a robot sprite to a goal.
